column1: # Where each Old English etymon in lex-ang.tsv was checked.
# The etymon column of lex-ang.tsv names the English word an Old English one
# became, and the product states it three ways, all strong: "This is the Old
# English word that became X" on the word page, "the direct ancestor of
# English X" in its description, "English X comes straight from Y" in the
# discoveries feed. So it has to be true of X, and X is where it is checked.
# On 2026-10-01 all 330 were read against etymonline, and against English
# Wiktionary where etymonline has no entry. 27 were not true as stated.
# Sixteen paired the English word with its Old English translation and
# called the translation its source: window is Old Norse vindauga, which
# replaced ēagþȳrel. Eleven named a compound or a derivative as though it
# were the word itself: gospel for spell, bishopric for rīċe. They are listed
# at the foot of this file with what the dictionary says, so that nobody
# Each line names the entries it was checked against, separated by spaces:
# tests/tools/ang-etymons.test.ts requires every etymon in lex-ang.tsv to have
# a line here citing that English word's own entry, and no line here to
# outlive its claim. It cannot tell an entry somebody read from one somebody
# typed: cite the ones actually opened. etymonline files neighbour and grey
# under neighbor and gray, and the test knows those two.
# What a descent survives, and what it does not
# It survives a cognate reshaping the word: sister, give and carve took a
# Norse form and are still the Old English words. It survives an inflected
# form of the word itself becoming the English one: shadow is the oblique
# case of sċeadu, numb the past participle of niman, former the comparative
# of forma. It does not survive "partly from", "probably", a compound that
# only contains the word, or an English word that only replaced it.
# Notes are not covered. Where a fetched entry contradicted or hedged a note,
# the note was rewritten and the entry is cited on its line; the other notes
# were read against their etymon's entry only.
# A numbered target is the second of two words with one spelling: rīċe² is
# rich, the adjective, and rīċe the realm. English Wiktionary gives the two
# separate etymologies, files both under "rice", and gives the adjective as
# the one that became rich. The number is part of the key, so this line can
# only vouch for the adjective. See lex-ang.tsv on homographs.
# Removed on 2026-10-01, with what the dictionary says
# Each was a claim lex-ang.tsv made; the row keeps a note where a true thing
#   boy       cnapa      knave       etym:knave — from late Old English cnafa, "probably related to Old English cnapa"; wikt:ang:cnapa gives only Middle English knape
#   lion      lēo        lion        etym:lion — late 12c., from Old French; "Old English had the word straight from Latin as leo"
#   egg       æġ         egg         etym:egg — from Old Norse; Old English æg gave Middle English eye, eai, which egg displaced
#   window    ēagþȳrel   window      etym:window — from Old Norse vindauga, "wind eye"; "It replaced Old English eagþyrl"
#   country   rīċe       bishopric   etym:bishopric — Old English bisceoprice, bishop + rice: a compound, not this word
#   money     feoh       fee         etym:fee — "the merger or mutual influence of two words, one from Old English, one from an Old French form"
#   question  āscung     asking      etym:asking — c. 1200, "replacing Old English ascunge", from ask
#   music     drēam      dream       etym:dream — "Much study has failed to prove that Old English dream is the source of the modern word"
#   dream     swefn      somnolent   etym:somnolent — from French and Latin somnolentus; wikt:ang:swefn shares only the root with somnus
#   anger     ierre      ire         etym:ire — c. 1300, from Old French ire, from Latin ira
#   gift      ġiefu      gift        etym:gift — from a Scandinavian source; giefu "is related to the Old Norse word"
#   weak      wāc        weak        etym:weak — from Old Norse veikr, "cognate with Old English wac"
#   sad       unrōt      sad         etym:sad — from Old English sæd, "sated, full"
#   close     clȳsan     close       etym:close — from Old French clos-; "also partly from Old English beclysan"
#   remember  ġemunan    mind        etym:mind — from Old English gemynd, a different word
#   catch     fōn        fang        etym:fang — Old English fang, a noun made from fon's past participle
#   almost    fulnēah    full nigh   no dictionary has "full nigh"; etym:nigh is from Old English neah
#   alone     āna        one         etym:one — from Old English an; etym:alone — from Old English all ana
#   hundred   hund       hundred     etym:hundred — from Old English hundred; "The common word for the number in Old English was simple hund"
#   hello     wes hāl    wassail     etym:wassail — "from Old Norse ves heill"; Old English wes þu hal "is not recorded as a drinking salutation"
#   goodbye   far wel    farewell    etym:farewell — Middle English, attested c. 1200; wikt:en:farewell has Old English only as "possibly" *far wel
# Replaced on 2026-10-01: the old etymon, the new one, and why
#   body      līċ        lychgate → lich      a compound of lich and gate; etym:lich is "a southern England dialectal survival of Old English lic"
#   shadow    sċeadu     shade → shadow       etym:shade is "from late Old English scead, also partly from sceadu"; etym:shadow is from its oblique cases
#   morning   morgen     morning → morn       etym:morning is a 13c. formation on morn; etym:morn is "from Old English … morgen"
#   story     spell      gospel → spell       etym:gospel is Old English godspel, god + spel; etym:spell (n.1) is "from Old English spell"
#   take      niman      nimble → numb        etym:nimble is from næmel, "related to niman"; etym:numb is "from past participle of nimen … from Old English niman"
#   first     forma      foremost → former    etym:foremost is from formest; etym:former is the "comparative of forme … from Old English forma"
#   village   þorp       thorpe → thorp       the headword both dictionaries use
#   very      swīþe      swithe → swith       wikt:en:swith, which gives swithe as a variant; etymonline has neither
